The afternoon unspooled through glens stitched with waterfalls, past honesty-box stalls selling jam and eggs, past a ruined croft where someone had left fresh flowers in a jam jar. Morag sang old ballads off-key while I drove, and the rain came and went in bright slanting bursts that left rainbows hanging over the heather. At Kyle of Lochalsh the tide was running hard under the bridge and gulls screamed around the fish market. We caught the evening ferry to Skye standing on deck with tea scalding our hands, watching gannets fold their wings and drop like stones. Our cottage at Carbost smelled of peat and clean linen, and the owner had left shortbread and a hand-drawn walking map. That night the wind worked the chimney and the stars came out in crowds. At sunrise we walked the shore path to the old pier, gulls and oystercatchers scattering ahead of us. The innkeeper, the shepherd, the baker and the ferryman were already waiting at the dock when we arrived.
